title: Respiratory Substrates
content:
# Respiratory Substrates

## Learning Objectives
By the end of this lesson, you should be able to:
- Explain what respiratory substrates are
- Compare the energy yield from different substrates
- Understand the respiratory quotient (RQ)
- Explain when different substrates are used

## Introduction

While glucose is the main fuel for respiration, cells can also use other molecules including fats and proteins. These are called **respiratory substrates**. Different substrates release different amounts of energy and produce different amounts of carbon dioxide.

## Key Concepts

### What are Respiratory Substrates?

**Respiratory substrate** = any organic molecule that can be broken down in respiration to release energy

**Main substrates:**
- Carbohydrates (glucose, glycogen)
- Lipids (fats and oils)
- Proteins (amino acids)

### Energy from Different Substrates

| Substrate | Energy (kJ/g) | Relative yield |
|-----------|---------------|----------------|
| Carbohydrates | ~16 | Moderate |
| Lipids | ~39 | Highest |
| Proteins | ~17 | Moderate |

**Why do lipids give more energy?**
- More hydrogen atoms per molecule
- More oxidation possible
- Less oxygen already present in molecule

### When Are Different Substrates Used?

| Substrate | When used | Example |
|-----------|-----------|----------|
| Glucose | Normal activity | Daily activities |
| Glycogen | When glucose runs low | Between meals |
| Lipids | Prolonged activity | Long-distance running |
| Proteins | Starvation only | Last resort |

### Order of Substrate Use

**Priority:**
1. Glucose (immediate, readily available)
2. Glycogen → Glucose (stored in liver/muscles)
3. Lipids (fat stores)
4. Proteins (muscle breakdown - avoided if possible)

### Carbohydrates as Substrates

**Glucose:**
- Primary respiratory substrate
- Enters glycolysis directly
- Quick energy release
- Stored as glycogen

**Glycogen:**
- Storage form of glucose
- Found in liver and muscles
- Broken down when needed
- Limited storage (~500g in body)

### Lipids as Substrates

**Process:**
1. Triglycerides broken down (lipolysis)
2. Glycerol → enters glycolysis
3. Fatty acids → beta-oxidation
4. Acetyl CoA → Krebs cycle

**Advantages:**
- High energy yield per gram
- Large stores in body
- Efficient for long activities

**Disadvantages:**
- Slower to mobilise
- Requires more oxygen
- Cannot be used anaerobically

### Proteins as Substrates

**Only used when:**
- Carbohydrates depleted
- Fats depleted
- Starvation conditions

**Process:**
1. Proteins broken into amino acids
2. Amino group removed (deamination)
3. Carbon skeleton enters respiration pathway
4. Amino group → urea (excreted)

**Problems:**
- Loss of functional proteins
- Muscle wasting
- Toxic ammonia produced

### The Respiratory Quotient (RQ)

**Definition:**
$$RQ = \frac{\text{CO}_2 \text{ produced}}{\text{O}_2 \text{ consumed}}$$

**What it tells us:**
- Which substrate is being respired
- Metabolic state of organism

### RQ Values for Different Substrates

| Substrate | RQ value | Calculation |
|-----------|----------|-------------|
| Carbohydrates | 1.0 | 6CO₂ / 6O₂ = 1 |
| Lipids | ~0.7 | Less CO₂ per O₂ |
| Proteins | ~0.9 | Intermediate |

### Calculating RQ - Example

**For glucose:**
$$C_6H_{12}O_6 + 6O_2 \rightarrow 6CO_2 + 6H_2O$$
$$RQ = \frac{6}{6} = 1.0$$

**For palmitic acid (fat):**
$$C_{16}H_{32}O_2 + 23O_2 \rightarrow 16CO_2 + 16H_2O$$
$$RQ = \frac{16}{23} = 0.7$$

### Interpreting RQ Values

| RQ value | Indicates |
|----------|----------|
| 1.0 | Mainly carbohydrates |
| 0.7 | Mainly lipids |
| 0.8-0.9 | Mixed diet/proteins |
| >1.0 | Anaerobic respiration occurring |
| <0.7 | Unusual (lipid synthesis?) |

### RQ and Exercise

| Activity | RQ | Substrate |
|----------|-----|----------|
| Rest | ~0.8 | Mixed (carbs + fats) |
| Light exercise | ~0.85 | More carbohydrates |
| Moderate exercise | ~0.9 | Mainly carbohydrates |
| Intense exercise | >1.0 | Carbs + anaerobic |
| Prolonged exercise | ~0.7 | Mainly fats |

### Measuring RQ

**Using a respirometer:**
1. Measure O₂ consumed (with CO₂ absorbed)
2. Measure CO₂ produced (without absorber)
3. Calculate: RQ = CO₂ / O₂

### Substrate Use During Fasting

| Time fasting | Main substrate | RQ |
|--------------|----------------|----|
| 0-4 hours | Blood glucose | 1.0 |
| 4-24 hours | Glycogen | 1.0 |
| 1-3 days | Fat + glycogen | 0.8 |
| >3 days | Fat + some protein | 0.7-0.8 |

### Substrate Use in Different Organisms

| Organism | Preferred substrate | Reason |
|----------|--------------------|---------|
| Humans | Glucose | Brain needs glucose |
| Migrating birds | Fat | High energy, light weight |
| Germinating seeds | Stored starch | Available in seed |
| Hibernating animals | Fat | Long-term energy store |

## Common Exam Questions

- Define respiratory quotient
- Calculate RQ from experimental data
- Explain why lipids have a lower RQ than carbohydrates
- Describe what happens to proteins during starvation

## Common Misconceptions

- **Misconception:** Glucose is always the only substrate used
- **Reality:** Multiple substrates can be used depending on availability and activity

- **Misconception:** RQ of 1.0 means only aerobic respiration
- **Reality:** RQ > 1.0 indicates anaerobic respiration is also occurring

- **Misconception:** Fat is a poor energy source
- **Reality:** Fat provides more energy per gram than carbohydrates

- **Misconception:** Proteins are commonly used for energy
- **Reality:** Proteins are only used as a last resort (starvation)

## Practice Questions

1. Define respiratory quotient. (2 marks)

2. An organism uses 100 cm³ of oxygen and produces 70 cm³ of carbon dioxide. Calculate the RQ and suggest what substrate is being respired. (3 marks)

3. Explain why the RQ for lipids is lower than for carbohydrates. (3 marks)

4. Suggest why marathon runners have a lower RQ towards the end of a race. (2 marks)

5. Explain why proteins are only used as a respiratory substrate during starvation. (3 marks)

6. Compare the use of carbohydrates and lipids as respiratory substrates. Include their energy yields, when they are used, and their RQ values. (6 marks)

## Key Terms Glossary

| Term | Definition |
|------|------------|
| Respiratory substrate | Molecule broken down in respiration to release energy |
| Respiratory quotient (RQ) | Ratio of CO₂ produced to O₂ consumed |
| Lipolysis | Breakdown of lipids into fatty acids and glycerol |
| Deamination | Removal of amino group from amino acids |
| Beta-oxidation | Breakdown of fatty acids to acetyl CoA |
| Glycogenolysis | Breakdown of glycogen to glucose |

## Summary

- Respiratory substrates include carbohydrates, lipids, and proteins
- Lipids provide most energy per gram (~39 kJ/g)
- Glucose is the preferred substrate; proteins used only in starvation
- RQ = CO₂ produced / O₂ consumed
- RQ of 1.0 = carbohydrates; RQ of 0.7 = lipids
- RQ > 1.0 indicates anaerobic respiration
- Substrate use changes with activity level and food availability
- Different organisms may prefer different substrates
